passage:
"Tenzin, what happened to your hair?" Binita stood in the bathroom doorway with a towel over her arm.
"It's just a streak, Ama. Blue. Like the prayer flags."
"Blue. Right." Binita came closer. "Did someone dare you?"
"No! My friends did theirs first, but I chose the colour myself. It washes out in a few weeks."
"And if the teacher says something?"
"Then I'll say it's temporary." Tenzin turned to the mirror. "Do you hate it?"
Binita tilted her head. "I'm surprised. Give me a minute." She touched the tip of the streak. "It's actually kind of nice with your eyes."
"Really?" Tenzin was already smiling.

qa.q: What colour is the streak in Tenzin's hair?
qa.a: The streak is blue, like the prayer flags.

qa.q: What might Binita be feeling as she looks at the streak?
qa.a: Surprise first, and perhaps some worry about school, but her curiosity and the way she touches the streak suggest she is warming to it.

qa.q: How could Binita respond so that Tenzin keeps talking to her?
qa.a: She can stay curious, ask about the choice, and treat the streak as an experiment rather than a sign of trouble.

qa.q: Why might Tenzin ask 'Do you hate it?'
qa.a: Tenzin cares about Ama's opinion and is a little nervous, since a new look can feel like showing a new side of oneself.

grounding: A teen tries a new hair colour as trial and belonging, and a parent responds with curiosity, not alarm.

passage: I went through phases that year. First it was black eyeliner and my brother's old hoodies. Then thrifted shirts two sizes too big, and a tiny silver stud in my nose that Mummy allowed after a long discussion. Gurpreet, my best friend since Class 6, said, "You look different every week." She didn't say it unkindly, but I got defensive. "I'm trying things," I told her. And that was really it. I wasn't sad or hiding. I was checking which version felt like me, and which one my new friends in the art club liked. Most of it has gone now. The stud stayed. - Madhuri

qa.q: What small piece of jewellery did Madhuri get?
qa.a: She got a tiny silver stud in her nose.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri feel defensive when Gurpreet spoke?
qa.a: She may have heard judgement in the remark, even though Gurpreet did not say it unkindly; Madhuri was in the middle of trying things and didn't want them dismissed.

qa.q: How could a friend respond to someone changing style often?
qa.a: Stay curious and supportive, ask what they like about each look, and treat it as exploring rather than as a problem.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt watching her friend change so often?
qa.a: She may have been surprised or a little unsure of what to expect, but her remark did not sound unkind, so she probably was simply noticing.

grounding: A teen tries on styles and identities as trial and belonging, not as proof of deeper trouble.

passage:
Coach's note - Harish, school band, Friday
Sahil turned up to rehearsal with bright blue hair. His mother had phoned me in the morning, worried. She asked if something was wrong, if he was "falling in with a bad crowd."
I watched him closely all week. He was on time, practised his drum part more than anyone, and joked with the juniors. The only change was the hair, and a new black band T-shirt.
When I asked him, he shrugged. "The drummer in my favourite band has blue hair. Also I wanted to see how I'd look. I might change it next month."
I called his mother back. I told her he seemed happy, focused and part of the group, and that trying a new look at sixteen is normal. We agreed to keep an eye on the bigger things, like sleep, mood and friends, not the colour.
Next week, three band members turned up with blue streaks.

qa.q: What colour was Sahil's hair?
qa.a: Bright blue.

qa.q: What was Sahil's mother feeling when she phoned?
qa.a: She was worried and anxious, afraid the blue hair meant something was wrong or that Sahil was falling in with a bad crowd.

qa.q: What did Harish do that helped?
qa.a: He watched Sahil's behaviour for a week, asked him directly, and reassured his mother that the hair looked like experimentation, while agreeing to watch mood and sleep.

qa.q: What would change if Sahil's mother had banned the hair colour straight away?
qa.a: Sahil might have felt judged and less willing to talk, over what was really just a trial and a sign of belonging to the band.

grounding: The coach's note shows a teenager experimenting with hair colour for belonging and self-exploration, and adults not treating it as proof of trouble.

passage:
Sunday
Tried on Dada's old corduroy jacket today, the one in the trunk. It's brown, too big in the shoulders, and it smells like mothballs and something like him. I wore it to the market and felt... more like me? I don't know.
Also tried a tiny silver stud in my ear. Clip-on for now. Zainab didn't laugh. She squinted and said, "The jacket, yes. The earring, maybe. Try it for a week."
Mummy asked at dinner, "Why the costume?" I said, "Just trying."
She looked worried for a second. Then she said, "Dada wore that jacket to every wedding for thirty years. It looks good on you."
I nearly cried.
I don't know yet which bits are me. Maybe the jacket stays and the earring goes. Maybe both stay. It's nice not to have to decide today.
- Zubin

qa.q: Where was Dada's old jacket kept?
qa.a: In the trunk.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling while wearing Dada's jacket?
qa.a: Zubin felt nostalgic and oddly more like the real Zubin, comforted by the smell and memory of Dada.

qa.q: What made Zainab's reaction supportive?
qa.a: Zainab didn't laugh and suggested trying the earring for a week, treating the style as an experiment rather than a problem.

qa.q: How might Mummy have seen Zubin's "costume" at first, and later?
qa.a: At first she looked worried, but she soon saw it as a loving link to Dada and told Zubin it looked good.

grounding: The diary shows a teenager trying on clothes and jewellery to explore identity, and family treating it as trial rather than trouble.

passage: When Jeevan came home from the barber in Kushalnagar with bleached orange tips and a tiny silver stud in one ear, Ajji put down her coffee. "Who are you trying to be? Is it those boys at the bus stand?" Jeevan's ears burned around the new stud. "It's just hair, Ajji." Tenzin, who had come along from the settlement to watch, shifted by the door. "Mine was green last year," he offered. "It washed out. My amala survived." Ajji didn't laugh. That evening Jeevan's father pulled an old album from the cupboard and put it on the table without a word. There he was in college, hair down to his shoulders and a bead necklace. Ajji peered at it and finally laughed. "I thought you'd joined a drama company." "I was trying things," Appa said. "Then I stopped. He will too, or he won't. Either is fine." Jeevan kept the stud. The orange lasted two weeks.

qa.q: What did Jeevan come home with from the barber?
qa.a: Jeevan came home with bleached orange tips and a tiny silver stud in one ear.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when Ajji asked 'Who are you trying to be?'
qa.a: Jeevan felt embarrassed and a bit defensive, ears burning, since the new look was just an experiment; there may also have been hurt at being linked to 'those boys'.

qa.q: How did Appa help settle the worry?
qa.a: He showed his own old college photo of trying out long hair and said Jeevan might stop or not and either was fine, treating the style as a trial, not trouble.

qa.q: What might Ajji have been worried about?
qa.a: Ajji seemed afraid the new look meant Jeevan was falling in with a bad crowd, until the old album showed it could simply be trying things.

grounding: It shows a teenager experimenting with hair and jewellery as trial and self-exploration, and a family seeing it is not proof of deeper trouble.
